entry.heading: Vagabond
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a long road from killing to living: strength that serves only the self is empty, and the warrior grows by facing fear, accepting limits, and learning to belong to the earth and to other people.

content.framing: Mixed: some encounters shown as exploitative or empty; framing to verify

frames.aligns: Evil is not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7): pride is humbled, killing for prestige leaves Musashi crippled and doubting; mercy to a defeated enemy (Inshun); a mentor who calls a violent youth to conversion (Takuan); the dignity of work in the farming arc.
frames.concerns: Message: salvation is framed as Zen enlightenment, judged with respect for "what is true and holy" in other religions (Nostra Aetate 2). Depiction: explicit sexual scenes and nudity (chastity and modesty, CCC 2521-2524); sexual coercion of Akemi (to verify); gore; the killing of a child.

frames.aligns: Struggle against the passions (anger, pride, fear); the elder-disciple bond (Takuan, Sekishūsai) resembles spiritual fatherhood; ascetic discipline; killing shown as wounding the killer, close to St. Basil's canon 13. No mockery of sacred things.
frames.concerns: Message: a non-Christian path to "enlightenment" offered as the goal. Depiction: guarding the senses (nepsis) makes explicit sexual imagery and sustained gore a serious concern.

frames.aligns: Sin's cost shown honestly; pride brought low; a turning from violence; hard work. Many Baptists distinguish depicting sin from endorsing it.
frames.concerns: Message: Buddhist enlightenment as the answer. Depiction: explicit sex and nudity and graphic killing weighed against Philippians 4:8. Soul liberty means each family decides; most would hold it back from younger teens.

frames.aligns: A clear arc from violence toward humility and service; honest picture of sin's cost; friendship and reconciliation (Musashi and Matahachi). Fits the "depicting is not endorsing" reading many evangelicals use.
frames.concerns: Message: Zen framing of the answer. Depiction: explicit sexual content and gore under Philippians 4:8 and Romans 14 conscience. No Plugged In review found.

frames.aligns: Pride and fear confronted; transformation of a "wild beast" of a man. No demons, magic or occult practice, so the "open door" concern is low.
frames.concerns: Message: Buddhist meditation and enlightenment offered as the path. Depiction: explicit sexual scenes and gore against holiness standards.

frames.aligns: Common grace: serious art by a non-Christian can show truth about pride and human limits; the sword's emptiness echoes Ecclesiastes. No images of God or Christ.
frames.concerns: Message: self-perfection through discipline rather than grace. Depiction: explicit sexual content falls under Westminster Larger Catechism Q139 ("lascivious... books, pictures").

frames.aligns: Law at work: no amount of skill satisfies Musashi; vocation and ordinary work (farming) honored, close to Luther's teaching on vocation.
frames.concerns: Message: enlightenment as self-achievement. Depiction: entertainment is adiaphora judged by love and conscience; explicit sexual content (sixth commandment) and violence. Range: LCMS and WELS families would often rate this Significant; ELCA families Discuss.

frames.aligns: Growth toward holiness of heart and life, read by analogy; turning from harm; social concern for villagers and an orphan.
frames.concerns: Message: holiness reached without grace. Depiction: Wesley's General Rules caution against diversions that do not "tend to the knowledge or love of God"; explicit sexual content and gore. Range: holiness churches (Nazarene, Wesleyan) Significant; UMC Discuss.

frames.aligns: A literary tradition (Lewis, Sayers) that judges works by how they frame good and evil; Vagabond frames killing for glory as empty; virtue, self-knowledge and reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Message: the spiritual answer is Zen. Depiction: explicit sexual content and gore, judged case by case; ACNA families likely more cautious than Episcopal ones.

frames.aligns: The story itself questions the sword: after the massacre Musashi doubts killing and turns to farming; humble labor and community.
frames.concerns: Message: violence shown as heroic is the central concern (nonresistance, Matthew 5:39); the story critiques killing yet keeps the sword at the center of the hero's identity, and the set-piece battles are drawn to thrill. Depiction: Old Order separation from worldly media; Mennonite Church USA families more open.

frames.aligns: Agency, self-mastery, repentance-like change, hard work and care for a child; "virtuous, lovely, or of good report" (Article of Faith 13) in its themes of humility and mercy.
frames.concerns: Message: a non-Christian spiritual answer. Depiction: For the Strength of Youth (2022) asks youth to choose media that invites the Spirit; explicit sexual content and graphic violence under a Mature rating. Members vary in strictness.

frames.aligns: Turn from violence toward simple rural life, work with the soil and care for a child, close to Adventist country-living counsel; violence shown with consequences. (from general knowledge; to verify)
frames.concerns: Message: non-Christian spirituality as the answer. Depiction: Fundamental Belief 22 asks for entertainment "of the highest quality"; Ellen White warned against fiction that excites the passions; explicit sexual content and gore. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Pride shown as empty; peace and honest work valued in the end; violence shown as destructive. (from general knowledge; to verify)
frames.concerns: Message: Buddhist teaching is presented as the way to truth, which Witnesses see as false religion; the hero's identity is still the sword. Depiction: jw.org counsel against entertainment featuring what God hates, especially violence (Psalm 11:5) and immorality (Galatians 5:19-21). (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Mind over fear: Musashi's growth comes as his thinking changes, which loosely echoes Mary Baker Eddy's stress on right thinking; fear named as the real enemy. (from general knowledge; to verify)
frames.concerns: Message: bodily wounds and death treated as real and final. Depiction: "Stand porter at the door of thought" (Science and Health 392): long dwelling on gore, injury and sexual content is something members guard against. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Critique of violence, ego and prestige; dignity of the disabled (Kojirō); care for the poor in the farming arc; interfaith respect for Zen.
frames.concerns: Message: women's limited roles; how the sexual exploitation of Akemi is framed (to verify). Depiction: gore and explicit sex weighed for age, not banned.

frames.aligns: Respect for life grows through the story; teachers and learning are honored; humility over pride (Proverbs 16:18); revenge (the Yoshioka feud, Osugi's grudge) shown as destructive, in line with Leviticus 19:18.
frames.concerns: Message: Buddhist enlightenment is the frame, though no idolatry is urged on the reader. Depiction: tzniut and nivul peh make explicit sexual content a serious concern; many Haredi homes would not admit secular manga at all; Modern Orthodox families selective.

frames.aligns: Respect for life, humility, teachers honored, revenge rejected; no antisemitic content.
frames.concerns: Message: Buddhist enlightenment as the frame. Depiction: no formal media rules; families apply modesty values to the explicit sexual content and weigh gore and the killing of a child for age.

frames.aligns: Critique of violence and ego; turn toward community and repair (tikkun olam) in the farming arc; no stereotypes of Jews.
frames.concerns: Message: women's narrow roles and exploitation (to verify). Depiction: informed autonomy; families usually read it as adult literature and weigh explicit content for age.

frames.aligns: Patience (sabr), humility and self-struggle (the greater jihad against the self, as often taught); killing for status shown as empty rather than heroic; respect for elders; honest work.
frames.concerns: Message: Buddhist enlightenment offered as the goal (tawhid). Depiction: explicit sexual content and nudity against lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) and haya; scholars differ on images, but none of the prophets are depicted.

frames.aligns: Close to Bhagavad Gita themes: the warrior's inner struggle, action without attachment to result, mastery of mind; Musashi's ego as the obstacle; killing for fame (outside dharma) shown as empty. Evokes strong rasa, valued in classical aesthetics.
frames.concerns: Message: little to raise. Depiction: some families apply the Gita's tamasic category (ch. 17) to gore and explicit sexual content.

frames.aligns: Central Zen themes: Takuan's teaching, emptying the mind, the self as the obstacle, suffering caused by craving fame; Inoue frames it as a path to enlightenment (Wikipedia); killing shown to create suffering.
frames.concerns: Message: some Buddhists note the samurai-Zen pairing can romanticize violence (a long-running debate). Depiction: right speech and mindfulness of what feeds the mind; gore and sexual content are things to watch.

frames.aligns: Purity, sincerity and harmony; the turn to rice farming and the land (ch. 303-327) fits Shinto's agrarian roots; respect for place and ancestors; no disrespect to shrines or kami. (from general knowledge; to verify)
frames.concerns: Message: Shinto is background, not engaged. Depiction: no doctrine on fiction; blood and death bring kegare (ritual impurity), and the story is full of both. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: The sant-sipahi (saint-soldier) ideal: spiritual discipline with martial skill; humility (nimrata); honest labor (kirat karni); the story treats ego (haumai), anger and lust as obstacles, not admirable. No Gurus depicted. (from general knowledge; to verify)
frames.concerns: Message: early Musashi kills for personal glory, which Sikh teaching rejects, though the story critiques it. Depiction: the Rehat Maryada does not address fiction; families value modesty and would weigh the sexual content. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Turning from conflict to service and work (work done in service is worship in Bahá'í writings); reconciliation; respect for other religions. (from general knowledge; to verify)
frames.concerns: Message: the hero's path runs through long stretches of killing. Depiction: Shoghi Effendi's call to a "chaste and holy life" warns against degrading entertainment; explicit sexual content. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Self-improvement, overcoming fear, raising ability and awareness; "Do not murder" (The Way to Happiness) matches the story's turn from killing. (from general knowledge; to verify)
frames.concerns: Message: killing for status in the early arcs, critiqued by the story. Depiction: no content code for fiction. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Reverence for nature and the land; harmony with seasons in the farming arc; personal responsibility for one's path; no portrayal of witches or pagans to object to. (from general knowledge; to verify)
frames.concerns: Message: the Rede ("harm none") conflicts with killing for fame, though the story shows its cost; Heathen paths honor warrior virtues more readily. Depiction: no central rule. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Critique of violent masculinity and status-seeking; respectful disability portrayal (Kojirō); class-aware turn to farmers.
frames.concerns: Message: women's narrow roles and sexual exploitation (Akemi, Okō; to verify); the male gaze in sexual scenes. Depiction: consent and age-appropriateness (Common Sense Media, AAP guidance) for the explicit content and the killing of a child.

frames.aligns: Meaning made in this life through effort, reason, self-knowledge and human ties; no supernatural claims; cruelty shown as costly.
frames.concerns: Message: a romanticized samurai myth. Depiction: free inquiry and opposition to censorship; gore and sexual content weighed for younger readers.

frames.aligns: "The good, the true and the beautiful": discipline, mastery, respect for elders and teachers, perseverance, humility, honest work, reconciliation with an old friend.
frames.concerns: Message: Musashi rejects institutions and bushido codes. Depiction: concern about gratuitous gore and explicit sexual content.

frames.aligns: Church of Satan (LaVey, The Satanic Bible) stresses self-mastery and personal achievement; Musashi's self-made path outside schools fits that, as does challenging hollow authority (Yoshioka). The Satanic Temple's tenets value compassion and justice. (from general knowledge; to verify)
frames.concerns: Message: the arc toward selflessness and Zen emptiness runs against LaVeyan self-indulgence; the killing of a child conflicts with the Eleven Rules (harm to children) and The Satanic Temple's first tenet. Depiction: no content code. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Free and responsible search for truth and meaning; interfaith respect; the inherent worth of every person, including the disabled and the defeated; turn from violence. (from general knowledge; to verify)
frames.concerns: Message: exploitation of women; narrow women's roles. Depiction: no formal rules; families weigh the explicit content for age and tend to read and discuss rather than avoid. (from general knowledge; to verify)

Dignity vs honor.evidence: The world runs on duels and school honor (the Yoshioka, v21-27) and Osugi's family grudge (ch. 113). The story honors Musashi's growth away from pride: sparing Inshun (ch. 71) and doubt after Ichijōji (ch. 224-242).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Musashi is a ronin who does not follow bushido; sword schools and clans are vain and self-protective, and individual teachers matter more than structures (Pragmatic lens).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Inherited family honor is shown as stubborn (Osugi), and kin ties are weak; the late arc honors belonging to the land and a village (farming with Iori, ch. 243 onward).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Teachers are honored and deferred to (Takuan, Sekishūsai, In'ei); inherited prestige is not (the Yoshioka). Peasants and villages are at the bottom of the social order.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Zen Buddhism is the spiritual voice (Takuan renames Musashi, ch. 21; the Hōzōin monks); Inoue wanted to show Musashi reaching enlightenment. "Heaven" frames the order of things.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Hard work, practice and humility are the path; farming is treated as worthy as swordsmanship (ch. 303-320). Musashi's early self-assertion is shown as empty.

folkways.japan: Early Edo samurai society, master-disciple relations, Zen practice and the dignity of rice farming are Japanese traditional values the series draws on directly; its critique of bushido and school prestige is its own.

entry.dominant: Dharmic (Zen Buddhist), Existentialism, Classical virtue ethics, with Might makes right present but critiqued.

entry.heading: Spy x Family (Tatsuya Endo)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is building a family, even an imperfect or "fake" one, and protecting the peace that lets children grow up without war.

content.frequency: Occasional; heavy in a few arcs
content.framing: Shown with consequences (Yor's work) / Neutral (spy action)

frames.aligns: Adoption and care for an orphan; self-giving love in the home; peace-making as a calling; war shown as suffering (Mission 62, Mission 99).
frames.concerns: The marriage begins as a deception and the story has not yet judged it; Yor's killing work is often played lightly; drunkenness as comedy (Missions 79-80).

frames.aligns: Love that grows through sacrifice; the family as a "little church"; grief for war's victims.
frames.concerns: Killing as a profession with little repentance shown (the tradition treats even killing in war as needing repentance, St. Basil canon 13); lying sits at the heart of the premise. Guarding the senses (nepsis) makes comic violence a point to talk through.

frames.aligns: Adoption and orphan care (James 1:27); a father who protects; war framed as evil.
frames.concerns: Lying in the home (Proverbs 12:22) is not yet judged; the mother's violence is played for laughs; drunkenness as comedy, a concern for the many Baptists who abstain. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Plugged In's reviewers call the series fun and say it encourages thinking about friendship and family. Adoption mirrors spiritual adoption (Romans 8:15).
frames.concerns: Plugged In flags deception, frequent violence, coarse language and "lightly bloody action," and notes other volumes can be more intense.

frames.aligns: Family as refuge; protection of children; love softening a hard heart.
frames.concerns: Anya's telepathy and Bond's foresight may raise spiritual-discernment questions, though the series frames them as a lab experiment (vol. 17), not spirits; drinking and drunkenness (many abstain); lying.

frames.aligns: Common grace: real goodness in a secular world; duty and diligence; lawful authority set against private violence and propaganda.
frames.concerns: Heroes' lies and killings rarely judged by the story; drunkenness.

frames.aligns: The family as a vocation where ordinary service matters; the state's sword versus private violence.
frames.concerns: Lying as a way of life; assassins working "for the nation."

frames.aligns: Love of neighbor, care for the weak, peace emphasis; characters slowly grow toward goodness.
frames.concerns: Drunkenness as comedy (historic abstinence; holiness churches ask members to abstain); killing for pay treated as a job.

frames.aligns: Found family; care for war victims; critique of war propaganda (Henry, Mission 99).
frames.concerns: Deception at the heart of the marriage.

frames.aligns: Henry's stand against war propaganda; the anti-war core; care for orphans.
frames.concerns: Violence is central to the heroes' jobs and often played for laughs, which reads as making it attractive; spies and assassins serve states; lying. Many conservative families avoid such media altogether.

frames.aligns: Strong family focus; parents who sacrifice; adoption.
frames.concerns: Drinking and smoking shown casually (Word of Wisdom); deception not yet judged (Articles of Faith 13 on honesty).

frames.aligns: Self-sacrifice for a child; peace over war; the home as central.
frames.concerns: Drinking played for laughs (members abstain, Fundamental Belief 22); killing for pay; lying. Ellen White's caution about fiction that excites the passions. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Care for orphans; honesty finally valued; the futility of war and of national rivalry.
frames.concerns: Violence as a main source of action and humor (Psalm 11:5); heroes serve rival states and spy agencies, at odds with political neutrality; drunkenness. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Love overcoming fear and mistrust; a child's goodness that holds the family together.
frames.concerns: Scenes of fear, war trauma and violence as mental influences to guard against; drinking (members abstain). (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Peace and justice emphasis; critique of militarism and propaganda; egalitarian domestic roles; found family.
frames.concerns: Comic violence; Yuri's harsh interrogation played lightly.

frames.aligns: Care for the orphan (Deuteronomy 10:18); memory of war; a dissenter jailed for speaking truth (Mission 99).
frames.concerns: Lying and killing as the heroes' work; drunkenness as comedy. Haredi families who restrict secular media would not read it; Modern Orthodox families are selective but engaged. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Care for the orphan; war shown as suffering; a just man punished for truth (Henry).
frames.concerns: Lying and killing; secret police echo real history. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam in the anti-war theme; found family; a stand against propaganda.
frames.concerns: Comic violence; secret police played partly for laughs. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Strong care for orphans (Qur'an 93:9); family duty; no sexual scenes reported by any guide consulted.
frames.concerns: Alcohol and drunkenness played for comedy (Missions 12-13 likely; 79-80); unrelated adults living as spouses under a false marriage; killing for pay.

frames.aligns: Duty (dharma) to family and nation; protection of a child; respect for elders and teachers (Henry).
frames.concerns: Killing and deceit as livelihood; drinking.

frames.aligns: Compassion growing from a selfish start; suffering caused by war; right intention slowly replacing a mission-only mind.
frames.concerns: The first, fourth and fifth precepts (non-harm, false speech, intoxicants) are all touched by the premise and rarely judged.

frames.aligns: Harmony in the household; gratitude and care between family members; no disrespect to kami or shrines.
frames.concerns: Sincerity (makoto) is central to the tradition, and the family is built on concealment. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Householder life (grihastha) and service to family; protecting the weak; standing up to injustice (Henry).
frames.concerns: Deception as a way of life; alcohol and smoking (rejected in the Rehat Maryada). (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Peace between nations and an end to war; unity of the family; education as the cure for war (Henry, Mission 97).
frames.concerns: Truthfulness is "the foundation of all human virtues," and the family is built on lies; drinking (forbidden). (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Care for children; family as the second dynamic; peace as survival for all.
frames.concerns: Anya and Bond as subjects of experiments framed as harm; killing and lying as jobs, against "do not murder" and "be worthy of trust." (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Chosen family; protecting the vulnerable; no stereotyped witches or pagans.
frames.concerns: Yor's killing work against "harm none." (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Found family over blood; role-swap in domestic work; critique of militarism, war propaganda, secret police and elite schools.
frames.concerns: Yuri's sister fixation as a joke; harsh interrogations played lightly; Common Sense Media rates diverse representations "very little."

frames.aligns: Human care, not faith, solves problems; reason and empathy; war shown as human suffering. Plugged In confirms no faith elements.
frames.concerns: Comic violence; Anya's telepathy is fiction, not pseudoscience presented as real.

frames.aligns: Two-parent home; discipline, school effort, good manners; duty; children protected.
frames.concerns: Marriage as a cover story; dishonesty in the home not yet resolved.

frames.aligns: Loyalty to those who earn it; protection of children (Eleven Rules); suspicion of state power and propaganda.
frames.concerns: The Satanic Temple's tenets on compassion and justice sit uneasily with killing for the state. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of an orphan; justice and peace; a family of choice.
frames.concerns: Comic violence and police brutality played lightly. (from general knowledge; to verify)

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Insult and grievance are rarely answered by personal vendetta. Henry's "elegance" (Mission 97) and his protest through words, not force (Mission 99), are honored. Yor's violence is framed as protecting others (cruise arc, Missions 43-57), not defending her name. Billy Squire's revenge is turned back by Anya's appeal (bus arc, vol. 11).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Duty, discipline and school effort are honored (Anya's Stella stars; Loid's self-control, Mission 62). State order is shown as both protective (Yuri's raid frees the hostages, vol. 11) and oppressive (Henry's arrest, Mission 99; secret police).

Civic vs kin.evidence: The chosen family comes first in daily life, and the Forgers protect each other above all. Loid's mission is for all children, not his own (Mission 62), and Henry chooses to teach so education can prevent war (Mission 97).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Eden's ranks (Stella Stars, Tonitrus Bolts) and respect for teachers are shown with some approval; old-money privilege and a munitions family shielded from discipline (Mission 97) are critiqued; Henry is forced out by a false bribery claim (Mission 124).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No faith shapes the plot; Plugged In reports "no elements of faith." Human care and reason solve problems; the schoolhouse "ghost" turns out to be a person (Mission 124). The nuclear-family form stays the goal, reached by an untraditional route.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Peace so children can grow up without war is the stated aim (Mission 62); warmth, food and home life carry the comedy. War memory (Missions 62, 99) keeps security in view. Domestic role swaps (Loid cooks; Yor fights) are treated with ease.

folkways.japan: The school-rank system, respect for teachers and the comedy of keeping up appearances for the group (the Eden interview, vol. 1) echo Japanese school and workplace norms rather than the story's own message, which is set in a fictional Cold War Europe.

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Secular humanism, Communitarianism (family and peace first), Traditionalism (family form), anti-war Utilitarianism and Pragmatism.

entry.heading: Vinland Saga
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A true warrior needs no sword: a good life means turning from violence and revenge, facing one's guilt, and building, by hard and patient work, a place where no one is enslaved and no one is an enemy.

frames.aligns: Revenge rejected; repentance and atonement central; evil shown so it is understood, not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7); dignity of slaves and enemies.
frames.concerns: Canute's vow to build paradise without God; Willibald is a drunken priest; graphic war violence (CCC 2525 on permissiveness).

frames.aligns: Repentance (metanoia) as a lifelong turning; tears and nightmares as the soul's awakening; love of enemies.
frames.concerns: Guarding the senses: the early arcs are long and bloody; Canute's defiance of God is left unresolved (to verify).

frames.aligns: A clear arc from sin to repentance; the father's sacrificial love; evil shown with consequences.
frames.concerns: Phil 4:8 test: much of vols. 1-8 is violent and grim; implied sexual violence; salvation is by Thorfinn's effort, not grace.

frames.aligns: Many evangelical readers see redemption, grace-like forgiveness and enemy-love (Matthew 5:44) in the story; it depicts sin without endorsing it.
frames.concerns: Graphic violence in the first arc; Christianity shown through flawed clergy and a king who rejects God.

frames.aligns: No occult practice shown as power; repentance and changed life; the cost of following peace.
frames.concerns: Norse religion and Valhalla appear as belief (not as real magic); berserker rage and drug-like mushroom; graphic violence.

frames.aligns: Total depravity shown honestly; common grace in a non-Christian author's moral seriousness.
frames.concerns: Redemption appears earned by works; Canute's rejection of God's sovereignty; WLC Q139 concern about violent and lustful images (implied sexual violence).

frames.aligns: Law and gospel themes: guilt crushes Thorfinn before he can live again; vocation as farmer and father.
frames.concerns: Little sign of grace from outside; violence level is a conscience matter (adiaphora); confessional families stricter.

frames.aligns: Sanctification as a long road of changed life; concern for slaves and the poor; social holiness in the Vinland plan.
frames.concerns: Holiness churches may weigh the violence against Wesley's General Rules; the UMC is more open.

frames.aligns: A literary epic that frames good and evil clearly, in the line of Lewis and Sayers; set in the era of English Christianity (Canute became king of England).
frames.concerns: Violence and grim tone in the first arc.

frames.aligns: Nonresistance is the core message: "I have no enemies" (ch. 96), the hero takes blows without striking back, and the Vinland plan bans weapons. Many Mennonite readers could see Matthew 5:39 in story form.
frames.concerns: Violence shown in detail for eight volumes before the turn; Old Order families avoid the medium itself; nonresistance is grounded in a father's ethic, not in Christ. Some readers would grade S on message.

frames.aligns: Repentance, restitution and family; a promised land settled in peace (a theme many members know from the Book of Mormon).
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth: entertainment that invites the Spirit; the graphic first arc and implied sexual violence.

frames.aligns: Peace, repentance, temperance contrasted with drunken warriors; Adventist noncombatancy.
frames.concerns: "By beholding we become changed": long war scenes and dark tone conflict with Fundamental Belief 22.

frames.aligns: Refusal to take part in war; condemnation of national and royal power struggles; violence shown as what God hates (Psalm 11:5) without glory in the end.
frames.concerns: Violent entertainment is discouraged; Norse gods and Christendom's clergy shown; graphic battles.

frames.aligns: Spiritual change transforms outward life; hatred dissolves when Thorfinn sees no enemies.
frames.concerns: Long dwelling on fear, killing and suffering; "stand porter at the door of thought" (Science and Health 392).

frames.aligns: Anti-war, anti-slavery, enemy-love; attention to the enslaved and the vulnerable.
frames.concerns: Women's stories are thin in early arcs (one review); the Vinland arc raises questions about settler colonialism.

frames.aligns: Revenge is forbidden (Leviticus 19:18) and the story agrees; teshuvah-like repentance; justice for the enslaved (Exodus 21).
frames.concerns: Christian theology framing much of the moral world; immodest scenes and implied sexual violence (tzniut); time spent on secular media.

frames.aligns: Teshuvah, the dignity of the enslaved, rejection of vengeance.
frames.concerns: Violence and implied sexual violence; Christian frame.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam in the dream of a land without war or slavery; ethics over ritual.
frames.concerns: Colonial setting in the last arc; violence level.

frames.aligns: Mercy over revenge, justice for slaves (freeing slaves is praised in the Qur'an, 90:13), repentance (tawbah).
frames.concerns: Alcohol and drunkenness; nudity and immodesty; Christian theological framing; the strict nonviolence differs from Islam's permitted just defense.

frames.aligns: Karma-like consequences: violence returns; renunciation of violence (ahimsa); duty to family.
frames.concerns: The Gita teaches that a warrior's duty can require fighting; Thorfinn rejects this; tamasic violence in the first arc.

frames.aligns: First precept (non-harm) as the story's goal; the cycle of hatred and revenge produces suffering; insight through suffering.
frames.concerns: Long violent sections; the protagonist's peace is relational and ethical rather than meditative.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) and gratitude; purification from past wrong; harmony with community and land.
frames.concerns: Blood and death (kegare) everywhere in the first arc; no kami or Japanese setting.

frames.aligns: Rejects vengeance for personal gain; the five vices (anger, ego) shown as destructive; equality of all people.
frames.concerns: Sikh teaching honors defending the oppressed by arms when needed (Guru Gobind Singh); Thorfinn's absolute nonviolence differs.

frames.aligns: Non-violence, the oneness of humanity and a multiracial peaceful community in Vinland; end of slavery.
frames.concerns: Violence and immodest scenes against a "chaste and holy life"; alcohol.

frames.aligns: "Do not murder," "Honor and help your parents," "Do not harm a person of good will" (The Way to Happiness); recovery from trauma through action.
frames.concerns: Glorified violence concern in the first arc; drunkenness.

frames.aligns: "Harm none" fits the turn away from violence; respect for land and Indigenous people in Vinland.
frames.concerns: Norse religion appears mainly as a warrior-death cult; contemporary Heathens may object to the stereotype of Norse faith as bloodlust.

frames.aligns: Anti-war, anti-slavery, critique of toxic warrior masculinity; dignity of every person.
frames.concerns: Female characters underdeveloped in early arcs (Wikipedia review); settler colonialism in the final arc; implied sexual violence.

frames.aligns: Moral change through reason, empathy and responsibility; a human-made good society; no supernatural rescue.
frames.concerns: Graphic cruelty in the first arc; religious themes may read as heavy to some.

frames.aligns: Fatherhood, family, hard work on the land, keeping one's word, honor.
frames.concerns: The story critiques warrior honor and royal authority; strict nonviolence may read as naive; some violence.

frames.aligns: Questioning arbitrary authority (Canute's challenge to God); compassion and justice (Satanic Temple Tenets 1-2); critique of religion used for power.
frames.concerns: Church of Satan accepts proportionate retaliation; Thorfinn's turn-the-other-cheek ethic runs against the Satanic Bible's stance; harm to children shown (child soldiers).

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity of every person, including slaves and enemies; justice, peace and a free search for meaning.
frames.concerns: Graphic violence for younger readers; colonial themes.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Blood revenge is the early Thorfinn the story rejects; "I have no enemies" (ch. 96) is the thesis. Thors' "a true warrior needs no sword" (ch. 16) and Hild's letting go of revenge are honored.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Kingship is shown as power that must stay violent to stay in place (Canute, vols. 13-14), and slavery is condemned. The Vinland settlement is a patient, ordered community, not a free-for-all.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Family is the moral anchor (Thors, Thorfinn's mother and sister, Gudrid and their child), but the goal is a place where no one is enslaved and no one is an enemy, extended to strangers.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Slavery is indicted (Arnheid and Gardar, ch. 87-93); Ketil's farm wealth built on slaves is critiqued. The settlement aims for a place without masters.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Christianity is treated with respect and questions (Willibald on love; Canute's defiance of God, ch. 39), and Thorfinn's arc reads as repentance and atonement. Norse Valhalla belief is answered, not honored.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Hard, patient work and farming are the path to peace (vols. 8-14, 24-29). Peace and care for others, not personal expression, are the goals.

folkways.japan: Set in Viking-age Europe, so few norms are directly Japanese; Yukimura's portrayal of repentance through patient labor, and the Japanese title of ch. 96 (無敵, both "invincible" and "no enemies"), carry a Japanese and Buddhist-tinged reading of nonviolence.

entry.dominant: Might makes right (critiqued), Christian (explored), Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism, Secular humanism. The series' pacifism is not a listed lens; it is carried by the Christian, Dharmic and Secular humanism rows (my own framing).

entry.heading: The Promised Neverland
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life means refusing to accept a system that treats people as food, refusing to leave anyone behind, and refusing to answer cruelty with extermination: Emma wants everyone to live, enemies included, and she pays for it herself.

frames.aligns: The dignity of every person against a system that treats children as products; self-giving love; mercy toward enemies; Isabella's late repentance. Evil is shown to be understood, not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: A god-like being who bargains and takes a "reward"; Ray's planned suicide and Peter Ratri's suicide (CCC 2280-2283); sustained horror for younger readers.

frames.aligns: Self-emptying love for the least; prayer-like gratitude for food (Sonju and Mujika); love of enemies; Isabella's turn as metanoia.
frames.concerns: Watchfulness (nepsis): long stretches of fear and predation; the god-figure is capricious, not good; suicide shown.

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil; sacrificial love; the shepherd who will not leave one sheep behind (Luke 15:4).
frames.concerns: Phil 4:8 test: horror is the main mood; salvation comes through a bargain and human effort, not grace; self-harm and suicide on the page.

frames.aligns: Many evangelical readers see salvation imagery: escape from bondage, a leader who will not leave anyone behind, a costly price paid for others (Beneath the Tangles, a Catholic writer on the anime: Emma's refusal to let her family die as a picture of God's will that all be saved). Sin is depicted, not endorsed.
frames.concerns: Horror intensity; the false "god" who demands payment; adults and religious-looking institutions as betrayers.

frames.aligns: Deliverance from bondage; courage and faith under threat; enemies shown mercy.
frames.concerns: The "open door" concern: man-eating demons, a supernatural being who grants wishes for a price, demon religious rites. The demons are biological creatures, not spirits (my own framing; to verify on the page).

frames.aligns: Common grace lets families value good art by non-Christians; total depravity echoed in every human institution; providence-like twists.
frames.concerns: The god-like being is drawn as a figure (second-commandment readers may note it, though it is not presented as God); salvation by human striving; sustained fear.

frames.aligns: A theology of the cross reading: the weak and doomed are saved by one who suffers for them; vocation as care of neighbor (the oldest children for the youngest).
frames.concerns: Grace versus works: Emma earns the new Promise; self-harm and suicide scenes.

frames.aligns: Social holiness: rescuing the oppressed, refusing to abandon the least; Isabella's change shows grace can reach the guilty.
frames.concerns: Holiness churches may weigh the horror against Wesley's rule on diversions; suicide content.

frames.aligns: In the Lewis and Sayers tradition, a dark fairy tale that frames good and evil clearly; love of enemies; costly hope.
frames.concerns: Strong fear content for younger children; a capricious god-figure.

frames.aligns: Emma's refusal of extermination and her search for peace with the enemy; community care for the youngest.
frames.concerns: Old Order groups avoid such media entirely. The Goldy Pond arc and Norman's raid present armed resistance as necessary and partly heroic.

frames.aligns: Family bonds as the highest value; agency (children choosing to act); sacrifice for others; a mother's late redemption.
frames.concerns: Does the horror "invite the Spirit" (For the Strength of Youth)? Self-harm and suicide on the page.

frames.aligns: Liberation of the oppressed; critique of systems that harvest the weak; dignity of the "other" (humans learn demons are people).
frames.concerns: Few concerns beyond intensity; some may question the "noble elite" Ratri framing (to verify).

frames.aligns: Self-sacrifice, care for children, trust, gratitude for food.
frames.concerns: "By beholding we become changed": sustained horror and predation; FB 22 asks for entertainment "of the highest quality"; supernatural bargain.

frames.aligns: Love, loyalty and protecting children are commended.
frames.concerns: jw.org asks whether entertainment features what God hates: violence (Psalm 11:5) and spiritism (Galatians 5:19-21). The god-like being who grants Promises and demon religious rites may be read as spiritism; violence is constant, though not glorified.

frames.aligns: Clear thinking and calm courage overcome fear; love casts out fear (1 John 4:18).
frames.concerns: "Stand porter at the door of thought": the series is built on fear, predation, drugging and disease (Norman's experiments); mental images of evil are dwelt on.

frames.aligns: Pikuach nefesh (saving life) and pidyon shvuyim (redeeming captives) drive the plot; gratitude before eating; teshuvah in Isabella.
frames.concerns: Many Haredi families restrict secular media; numbered children shipped to slaughter may echo the Holocaust for some readers (my own framing); a god-figure is drawn; suicide.

frames.aligns: Saving life, redeeming captives, ethical treatment of the other.
frames.concerns: Holocaust echoes (numbered necks, "shipping"; my own framing); horror intensity; a bargaining deity.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam: repairing a broken system rather than escaping alone; coexistence with the other; informed choice.
frames.concerns: Holocaust-like imagery should be discussed with care (my own framing); self-harm scenes.

frames.aligns: Protecting orphans (a strong Qur'anic theme, e.g. 93:9); mercy, justice, gratitude for provision; oppression condemned.
frames.concerns: A god-like being is drawn and bargains; demons who eat humans and demon worship; horror; suicide (Qur'an 4:29).

frames.aligns: Dharma of protection; ahimsa in Emma's refusal to destroy the demons; demons (like rakshasas) shown as capable of change; karma in Peter Ratri's end.
frames.concerns: Tamasic content (fear, darkness) for some families; suicide.

frames.aligns: Compassion for all beings, including the demons who eat humans; gratitude for the life one eats (Sonju and Mujika's lessons, vol. 6); breaking a cycle of hatred; non-attachment in Emma's ending.
frames.concerns: Observance-day and monastic precepts avoid entertainment; fear and killing shown.

frames.aligns: Seva and protection of the weak; courage (the warrior-saint ideal); ego and greed (Peter Ratri) shown leading to ruin.
frames.concerns: Little beyond intensity; the five vices are not admired.

frames.aligns: Unity of peoples, ending prejudice between humans and demons, consultation and justice.
frames.concerns: The "chaste and holy life" counsel may weigh against sustained horror.

frames.aligns: Gratitude for food and life (the itadakimasu spirit in Sonju's teaching); sincerity (makoto) in Emma; kami-like and oni figures common in Japanese culture.
frames.concerns: The god-figure "Him" and the hunting grounds may be read as impurity (kegare) themes; little conflict with Shinto values.

frames.aligns: "Harm none" ethic in Emma's choices; the cycle of life and death treated seriously; no stereotyped witches.
frames.concerns: Few concerns; the predation theme.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness precepts "Safeguard and improve your environment" and "Do not harm a person of good will"; children's self-determination; drug experiments on children condemned (vol. 14).
frames.concerns: Violence; Isabella complicates "Honor and help your parents."

frames.aligns: Children's agency; critique of exploitative systems and hereditary elites; empathy for the "other"; a girl leads.
frames.concerns: Self-harm depictions for younger readers; few women in power besides the Moms (to verify).

frames.aligns: Reason, planning and evidence win the escape; questioning inherited myths (the Promise); human dignity; rejection of genocide.
frames.concerns: The final solution depends on a supernatural being (a deus ex machina for some readers); the price Emma pays is arbitrary.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, duty, sacrifice for family and the young; a mother's final protective act; courage.
frames.concerns: All adult authority is shown as betrayal for most of the story; the institution is the enemy.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity of every being; justice for the oppressed; free search for truth (questioning the Promise).
frames.concerns: Age-appropriateness of self-harm scenes.

frames.aligns: Questioning and overthrowing an unjust order and its god-sanctioned "Promise"; reason and planning; compassion and justice (Satanic Temple Tenets 1-2).
frames.concerns: Harm to children (Eleven Rules) is central, though condemned; Emma's mercy toward enemies differs from the Satanic Bible's acceptance of proportionate retaliation.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Emma refuses to answer cruelty with extermination and talks Norman out of genocide (vol. 18). Isabella, who caged the children, is given repentance (ch. 177).

Order vs freedom.evidence: The story celebrates refusing a system that farms people (the escape, ch. 32-37; the new Promise, ch. 134-143). Freedom is won by planning and trust, not by tearing down all order.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Sibling-like chosen family drives the plot (no one left behind, even the four-year-olds), but Emma extends care to demons and strangers too: "everyone."

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Hereditary order (the Ratri clan, Peter Ratri; the demon aristocracy) is condemned and destroyed (vols. 11, 17-20). The children's leadership is shared among Emma, Ray and Norman.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: The escape is won by reason, testing assumptions and trading information. Sincere demon faith is honored (Sonju and Mujika, ch. 38-52), and the ending rests on a god-like being's bargain.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival and protecting the youngest dominate. The goal of a life where no one is food, and Emma's hope, add some weight to quality of life.

folkways.japan: Ranking children by test scores, with the lowest harvested first, echoes Japanese exam pressure; Shirai said the idea was meant to prompt reflection on society, not as a direct critique. The orphanage's "Mom" and "Sister" roles draw on Western Christian imagery rather than Japanese norms.

entry.dominant: Collectivism / authoritarianism (critiqued), Utilitarianism (critiqued), Secular humanism, Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics. "Anti-exploitation" is not a listed lens; it is carried by the Critical theory and Marxism rows (my own framing).

entry.heading: Blue Lock
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: Find what only you can do and pursue it without apology. Hunger to win, honest self-analysis and constant adaptation make you great. Others are rivals to learn from and "devour," and teamwork is valuable when it serves the strongest individual.

content.frequency: Pervasive outside the book; recurring inside

frames.aligns: Excellence and use of one's gifts (the parable of the talents); perseverance; honest self-examination; Kuon's betrayal framed as wrong and followed by effort to make amends.
frames.concerns: The story teaches self-assertion over solidarity and treats others as tools ("devour" them); pride is a capital sin, and the Church's media documents ask that media serve human dignity and the common good. Frequent f-words and "goddamn" in the dialogue.

frames.aligns: Discipline and ascetic-like training; facing one's weaknesses honestly.
frames.concerns: The Fathers count pride and vainglory among the most dangerous passions, and the story makes them the engine of growth. Watchfulness (nepsis) asks what a steady diet of "monster ego" imagery forms in a young reader.

frames.aligns: Hard work, self-discipline, using gifts fully; cheating shown as wrong.
frames.concerns: Philippians 2:3 ("Do nothing out of selfish ambition or vain conceit") runs directly against the story's thesis. Frequent f-words and "goddamn" (Ephesians 4:29; the Third Commandment). Views vary by congregation because each church is self-governing.

frames.aligns: Perseverance, excellence "as working for the Lord" (Colossians 3:23), learning from failure.
frames.concerns: Selfish ambition presented as the virtue; others treated as stepping stones. Many evangelicals distinguish depicting sin from endorsing it; here the story endorses ego, so it is a message issue. Profanity.

frames.aligns: Boldness, confidence, refusing to be passive; discipline.
frames.concerns: Self-exaltation as the path to power; divine and royal titles for star players. No occult practice; the "Awakening" auras with flaming-eyed skulls, a Buddha quote and karma talk (Plugged In, film) are minor points some families may note. Profanity. Views range between churches.

frames.aligns: Common grace lets families value a well-made sports story by non-Christians; the story is honest about human ambition and rivalry.
frames.concerns: Self-glory as the chief end, against "man's chief end is to glorify God" (Westminster Shorter Catechism Q1).

frames.aligns: Entertainment as adiaphora; vocation; honest admission of weakness and failure.
frames.concerns: Self-justification by performance runs against grace alone: worth in Blue Lock is earned by scoring, and losers are "trash." LCMS and WELS families tend to be more cautious than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Discipline, growth, perseverance.
frames.concerns: Wesley's question whether a diversion can be "used in the name of the Lord Jesus"; holiness churches would weigh self-exaltation and profanity heavily; the United Methodist Church is much more open.

frames.aligns: Honesty, discipline, avoiding substances and occult content.

frames.concerns: The thought the story cultivates is self-centered and fear-driven (fear of elimination); "Stand porter at the door of thought" asks what fills the mind.

frames.concerns: Humility (anavah) is a central trait; Pirkei Avot 4:1 ("Who is honored? One who honors others") inverts the program's values. Harsh insults (onaat devarim). Many Haredi homes restrict secular media like this; Modern Orthodox families are selective.

frames.concerns: Humility and kind speech; others as tools.

frames.concerns: Tikkun olam and the dignity of each person: the eliminated players are discarded.

frames.aligns: Striving for excellence (ihsan), discipline, honest effort, perseverance.
frames.concerns: Arrogance (kibr) is strongly condemned in the Qur'an and hadith; the story treats self-exaltation as virtue. Insults and profanity.

frames.aligns: Svadharma: finding one's own nature and role; disciplined action; intense focus (Isagi's "flow").
frames.concerns: The Gita teaches action without attachment to the fruits (2:47) and warns against ahamkara (ego); the story makes desire for victory and ego the fuel. Rajasic qualities (passion, rivalry) dominate.

frames.aligns: Right effort, concentration and honest self-observation; the "flow" state resembles absorption.
frames.concerns: The series explicitly cultivates ego and craving for victory, the roots of suffering in Buddhist teaching (Four Noble Truths; anatta, non-self); rivals are to be "devoured." This is a central message conflict, though nothing is graphic.

frames.aligns: Discipline, courage, standing up for oneself.
frames.concerns: Haumai (ego) is one of the five vices and the core obstacle to liberation; the frame guide notes concern when the five vices are "shown as admirable," and the story is built on admiring ego and anger.

frames.aligns: Excellence, developing one's capacities, unity across nations (foreign players shown positively).
frames.concerns: 'Abdu'l-Bahá taught that the "struggle for existence" is the source of conflict and that cooperation is the basis of human progress (from general knowledge; to verify); the story is a struggle for existence among teens.

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto) of effort; purity of dedication; national community.
frames.concerns: The story is an explicit critique of harmony (wa) and group belonging, values that shrine tradition expresses and reinforces; gratitude is rare. No disrespect to shrines or kami. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Personal will and empowerment, self-knowledge, transformation.
frames.concerns: The Rede ("harm none"): the program harms players' futures; little reverence for nature. No portrayal of witches or pagans.

frames.aligns: Competence, self-determinism, personal survival (the first dynamic), discipline and training; no psychiatry content. The Way to Happiness precept "Be competent."
frames.concerns: The eight dynamics also include family, group and humankind; the story ranks the group dynamic below the self. The church's own materials say little about anime.

frames.aligns: Critique of conformity; foreign characters shown positively; some critique of the football establishment.
frames.concerns: At the message level, an extreme-competition, winner-take-all system run on minors is presented as admirable; critics read it as promoting hierarchy and hyper-competition (The Daily Campus). Almost no women.

frames.aligns: Self-determination, reason and analysis (Isagi wins by thinking), merit, critical view of tradition and authority.
frames.concerns: Cruelty toward youths (lifetime bans, humiliation) is justified by results; dignity of the eliminated players is ignored.

frames.aligns: Meritocracy, discipline, competition, excellence, national pride (the goal is a World Cup win for Japan), personal responsibility.
frames.concerns: The story rejects inherited institutions (the football establishment, team harmony, seniority) and puts self above duty.

frames.aligns: Free search for one's own path; critique of conformity.
frames.concerns: The inherent worth and dignity of every person versus a system that discards losers; the interdependent web versus "devour your rivals."

frames.aligns: The Church of Satan treats rational self-interest as a virtue, sees each person as their own god, rejects false humility and values the strong, self-made individual; Blue Lock's creed of ego, self-knowledge and "becoming the best" is close to this. Rejection of the conformist establishment fits both groups. (Range: Church of Satan near S; The Satanic Temple lower.)
frames.concerns: The Satanic Temple's tenets stress compassion, justice and the dignity of others; Kaiser's cruelty and the treatment of eliminated players would concern TST readers.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Pride and the hunger to "devour" rivals are honored, and Rin's rage at Sae (ch. 115 onward) fuels his game. But disputes are settled on the pitch under the rules, and Kuon's cheating is condemned (First Selection, ch. 18-25).

Order vs freedom.evidence: The story celebrates the individual striker over team harmony (Ego's founding speech, ch. 1-3). Ego himself is an authoritarian figure inside a locked facility, so freedom is pursued through a harsh, rule-bound program.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty goes neither to family nor clan: kin ties appear mostly as wounds (the Itoshi brothers) and friendship is secondary to ego (Nagi leaves Reo, Second Selection). The program's goal is a national team, not a family.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Rank is everywhere (ranking screens, NEL bids, "emperor" and "god" titles, ch. 155 onward), but it is earned by results. Seniority and the football association's bureaucracy are critiqued.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No faith appears. Isagi grows through analysis, "formulas" and copying what works (Pragmatic lens). Traditional Japanese team harmony is presented as the cause of failure (ch. 1).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: The life message is "find what only you can do and pursue it without apology," a strong self-expression value. The setting is a survival contest with lifetime bans for losers (ch. 1-3), which keeps it near the middle.

folkways.japan: The series is an argument with Japanese norms; Kaneshiro says frustration with Japanese society shaped the focus on ego. Team harmony (wa), seniority and self-effacement are the values it pushes against, so readers from more individualist cultures may find its "ego" less radical than Japanese readers do.

entry.dominant: Existentialism (self-creation), Expressive individualism, Pragmatism, Might makes right ("skill makes right"), Classical virtue ethics; Communitarianism and Confucian-style harmony critiqued.

entry.heading: Death Note (Tsugumi Ohba and Takeshi Obata)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: The story shows a life spent claiming the power to judge others, and lets the reader watch where that leads. Ohba's own stated takeaway is: "Humans will all eventually die, so let's give it our all while we're alive" (Wikipedia, citing Ohba).

content.frequency: Constant (deaths every few chapters), mostly non-graphic

frames.aligns: The ruin of a proud man who makes himself judge of life and death; the innocent suffer from his "justice"; lawful authority prevails. Evil is shown in order to be understood, not made finally attractive (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: No repentance or grace; the "Mu" rule denies judgment and afterlife; Light's glamor can invite admiration. Coerced suicides and death gods weigh as depiction; many parishes would treat it as older-teen reading.

frames.aligns: Light as a picture of the passions, above all pride, and of a man refusing repentance; an Orthodox writer at Geeks Under Grace reads it as "the throne without the Cross."
frames.concerns: No hope of resurrection in the story's rules; death gods taken seriously as spirits; guarding the senses (nepsis) weighs on the long dwelling with a killer's mind.

frames.aligns: Clear arc from sin to ruin (Galatians 6:7); deception exposed; a thoughtful teen can discuss justice and the death penalty.
frames.concerns: A human claiming divinity is punished, but no gospel answer is given; the "Mu" ending; death gods. Profanity in the Viz text and coerced suicide fail many families' Philippians 4:8 test. Views vary by congregation.

frames.aligns: Plugged In praises the "compelling plot" and "conversations on morality and justice"; Christian reviewers read Light as a man seizing God's throne and falling.
frames.concerns: Plugged In warns of "spiritual themes, violence, and language" and apple and Eden imagery (anime). Range is broad, from churches that skip it to churches that use it for worldview talks.

frames.aligns: The man who takes a death god's power is destroyed by it.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": a supernatural death god who gives a human power to kill, and a notebook that works like a curse, are shown without any power of God against them.

frames.aligns: Light as a study in total depravity: a gifted, "good" student whose heart turns to self-worship; through common grace, a non-Christian story tells the truth about sin and the magistrate's sword.
frames.concerns: No grace or providence named; constant lying by the protagonist; coerced suicides (self-murder, WLC Q136).

frames.aligns: Two kingdoms: God works through lawful authority (police, courts), and Light usurps it; the law exposes him in the end.
frames.concerns: The story shows law and judgment but no gospel. LCMS and WELS families may be more cautious than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: "Do no harm" set against a man who does harm for "good"; Soichiro's integrity.
frames.concerns: Light refuses every chance to turn back, and the story offers none; profanity; holiness churches stricter than the UMC.

frames.aligns: Moral crime fiction in the Sayers tradition, judged by how it frames good and evil; lawful authority (Article 37) frames the duel.
frames.concerns: The nihilist "Mu" close; Light's glamor. ACNA families may be more cautious than Episcopal families.

frames.aligns: Violence and the will to punish shown as a trap that consumes the one who uses it; a critique of the death penalty.
frames.concerns: The heroes also use deception, confinement and guns; no peaceful alternative is shown. Conservative groups avoid such media; MC USA families may read it as a critique of capital punishment.

frames.aligns: Agency and its consequences; honesty (Article of Faith 13) as what finally defeats a liar.
frames.concerns: The "Mu" rule against the plan of salvation; no repentance. Coerced suicide, profanity and the body count weigh against media that invites the Spirit.

frames.aligns: Pride and self-made godhood brought to ruin; deception exposed.
frames.concerns: Death gods and a spirit realm (spiritualism is strongly rejected); the "Mu" rule shares the teaching that the dead are unconscious but denies resurrection. Ellen White's caution about fiction that excites the passions. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Human attempts to rule and judge end in ruin; no hellfire (Ryuk: "no heaven or hell").
frames.concerns: Death gods as real spirits granting power (spiritism, a major concern in jw.org counsel); death as final with no resurrection hope; violence. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Truth exposes error; the deceiver's power proves empty.
frames.concerns: Death presented as real and final, against the teaching that life is spiritual; long dwelling on fear and death as mental influences. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: A sharp critique of the death penalty, vigilantism, surveillance and populist media fits the peace-and-justice focus.
frames.concerns: Women defined by love for Light (AnimeFeminist); suicides without mental-health framing.

frames.aligns: Respect for life and due process; the danger of a man who makes himself an idol, brought down.
frames.concerns: Taking life outside lawful courts is never redeemed; a human claiming godhood. Coerced suicide and death gods; Haredi homes would avoid it. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Due process; the idolatry of power exposed.
frames.concerns: Suicide (traditionally forbidden); the "Mu" ending. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Ethical monotheism's warning against self-deification; critique of vigilante justice and surveillance.
frames.concerns: Flat women; suicides. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Unjust killing is grave and arrogance (kibr) leads to ruin; a human calling himself god (shirk) is destroyed.
frames.concerns: The story ends by denying the afterlife and divine judgment ("Mu"); suicide shown.

frames.aligns: Karma-like return: Light's actions bring his own end; satya (truth) defeats deception.
frames.concerns: Ego (ahamkara) never overcome; ahimsa; respect for parents broken.

frames.aligns: Karma-like logic; attachment to power and self drives suffering; Ryuk's detachment echoes impermanence.
frames.concerns: Constant false speech and killing (first and fourth precepts); the "Mu" ending can read as nihilism rather than Buddhist emptiness, though "mu" is also a Zen term.

frames.aligns: Death gods are folk figures, not kami; impurity and disorder end in ruin; sincerity (makoto) defeats deceit.
frames.concerns: Death and corpses (kegare) as constant imagery. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Ego (haumai) shown as the root of ruin; justice belongs to God, not to a self-made judge.
frames.concerns: Ego, anger and pride shown at length in an attractive lead; suicides. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Justice requires lawful institutions; the would-be judge falls.
frames.concerns: No spiritual hope; violence against the commitment to non-violence. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: "Do not murder" upheld by the plot; "be worthy of trust" set against Light's lies.
frames.concerns: Death as final nothingness contradicts the teaching of the immortal thetan. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: The threefold-return idea that harm comes back to the one who does it; death figures shown as folklore.
frames.concerns: Death gods as mere tools of harm. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: A sharp critique of vigilante "justice," the death penalty, mass surveillance and populist media.
frames.concerns: Flat female characters (AnimeFeminist); suicides without safe-messaging framing; police torture-like methods shown as clever; no LGBTQ+ characters (CSM).

frames.aligns: Reason, evidence and due process win; human life defended without religious grounding; no supernatural rescue.
frames.concerns: The glamor of a clever killer.

frames.aligns: Law and order matter; the police and a good father (Soichiro) are honorable; evil is defeated in the end.
frames.concerns: The glamor of a teen killer; the story's ambiguity about justice; Light deceives his father.

frames.aligns: A warning against anyone who makes himself god over others and against blind followers (the Kira cult).
frames.concerns: Church of Satan teaching accepts harsh retribution, so some may sympathize with Light's goal; The Satanic Temple's tenets on compassion and justice fit the critique. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Worth of every person, including criminals; justice through fair process.
frames.concerns: Flat women; suicides. (from general knowledge; to verify)

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Private judgment and killing are the story's target: Light's vigilante "justice" ends in exposure and death (ch. 103-107). Soichiro and the task force, who stand for rule of law, duty and honesty, are the moral center.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Law and due process are endorsed over one man's will. L's surveillance and confinement of suspects (Misa, ch. 33-35) are questioned, so order is honored but not without limits.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Rules are meant to apply to all, including family: Soichiro serves the investigation even as it points at his son. Light risks his father and sister (vols. 7-9), a betrayal of kin the story condemns as part of his corruption.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Light's claim to be "god of the new world" (ch. 1-2) is the root wrong; no person is above the law. The police chain of command and the Wammy's House succession (Near, Mello) are shown neutrally.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Religious language belongs to the villain and his cult (Mikami, ch. 83; the Kira worshippers, ch. 108). The "Mu" rule offers a naturalist note, and the duel is won by reason and investigation.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Crime, safety and deterrence are the central question; a frightened public accepts a killer who promises security (Pragmatic lens). Ohba's takeaway, "let's give it our all while we're alive," adds a modest self-expression note.

folkways.japan: Capital punishment, a powerful police bureaucracy and the public's quiet approval of Kira reflect debates in Japan, which keeps the death penalty; scholar Jolyon Baraka Thomas reads the cult elements against the 1995 Tokyo sarin attack. Soichiro's quiet devotion to duty echoes Japanese workplace norms.

entry.dominant: Utilitarianism (critiqued), Nihilism (explored), Might makes right (critiqued), Christian (explored, mostly as imagery and structure), Existentialism (explored).

entry.heading: Naruto (Masashi Kishimoto, 1999-2014)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is one where you never give up, earn the recognition of others through effort and loyalty, and break cycles of hatred by understanding and forgiving even your enemies.

frames.aligns: Love of enemies and redemption of villains (Gaara, Nagato, Obito); an outcast child's dignity; self-gift for friends; revenge shown as a trap.
frames.concerns: Voyeurism treated as a lovable quirk (Jiraiya); spirit summoning and reanimation, judged by framing; suicide in backstories (Sakumo).

frames.aligns: Forgiveness of enemies and repentance of villains echo theosis; self-sacrifice for friends.
frames.concerns: Evil spirits are taken as real, so a demon fox sealed in a child, spirit summoning, reanimated dead and a death-god cult read as more than fantasy for many families. Constant killing, which the tradition holds calls for repentance even in war; guarding the senses (nepsis).

frames.aligns: Perseverance, loyalty, a hero who refuses revenge (Romans 12:19). Grace-like acceptance of an outcast (Beneath the Tangles reads Iruka's acceptance through Ephesians 2).
frames.concerns: Spells, summoning and spirits (Deuteronomy 18:10-12); a peeping mentor shown as wise; Tsunade's drinking played for laughs, a concern for teetotal Baptists.

frames.aligns: Servant leadership, grace before merit, forgiveness of enemies (Beneath the Tangles). Many evangelicals accept Tolkien/Lewis-style fantasy magic.
frames.concerns: Chakra, summoning and reanimating the dead may read as spirit contact rather than Tolkien-style magic. Fan-service gags.

frames.aligns: Courage, loyalty, and a hero who will not take revenge.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": a demon-like beast sealed in a child, the Jashin blood ritual, spirit summoning and reanimation are often a strong concern even in fiction. Sexual gags and alcohol.

frames.aligns: Common grace: a non-Christian work shows real goods such as sacrifice and forgiveness. Every main character is flawed, which fits total depravity; villains are not simply monsters.
frames.concerns: Occult imagery; a lascivious mentor (WLC Q139); Sakumo's suicide (WLC Q136).

frames.aligns: Law and gospel: Naruto cannot earn acceptance by effort alone; it comes first from Iruka. Two kingdoms: rulers bear a sword and can abuse it (Danzo).
frames.concerns: Occult elements (usually adiaphora in fiction, with care); comic nudity.

frames.aligns: Prevenient grace: an outcast is loved before he changes. Social holiness: clan discrimination and secret violence challenged. Strong peace theme.
frames.concerns: Tsunade's drinking (holiness churches ask members to abstain); comic nudity.

frames.aligns: Deep roots in fantasy literature (C.S. Lewis); forgiveness, sacrifice, reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Comic nudity; occult-flavored powers, judged by framing.

frames.aligns: The central claim, that revenge must end and enemies be understood, is close to nonresistance.
frames.concerns: Yet nearly every conflict is settled by combat, and fighting is heroic. Conservative groups avoid much fantasy media and value separation from "the world."

frames.aligns: Family and sacrifice; forgiveness; respect for teachers; the ending's marriages and children.
frames.concerns: A peeping mentor shown as wise; alcohol played for laughs (Word of Wisdom); spirit contact.

frames.aligns: Forgiveness over revenge; self-sacrifice; peace.
frames.concerns: Reanimated dead and spirits of the dead shown as real conflict with the teaching that the dead sleep (Fundamental Belief 26); drinking; Ellen White's caution about fiction. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Ending the cycle of war; mercy to enemies.
frames.concerns: Spiritism (summoning, reanimation, a death-god cult) is a major concern in jw.org counsel; violence as the main action (Psalm 11:5); loyalty to a military village. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Love and understanding overcoming hatred; an outcast's true worth seen.
frames.concerns: Fear, death and despair as recurring mental imagery; drinking. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Social justice: criticism of war, clan discrimination, secret police and child soldiers; reconciliation with enemies.
frames.concerns: Gender roles (women as healers and wives); the Killer Bee stereotype CSM flags; fat jokes; harassment humor (Jiraiya).

frames.aligns: Respect for teachers and parents (Exodus 20:12); breaking cycles of revenge (Leviticus 19:18).
frames.concerns: Sorcery and spirit summoning (Deuteronomy 18); mocking speech (fat jokes) as lashon hara-like; nudity gags against tzniut. Haredi homes would avoid it; Modern Orthodox families are selective. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Respect for life and teachers; the end of revenge.
frames.concerns: Spirit summoning; nudity gags; mocking speech. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam in the anti-war theme; empathy for the outsider.
frames.concerns: Stereotypes (Killer Bee); gender roles. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Mercy, patience (sabr), care for orphans (Qur'an 93:9), keeping promises, forgiveness over revenge (42:40).
frames.concerns: Alcohol and gambling played for laughs (5:90); sihr and spirit summoning (2:102); Shinto deity names, which some read as shirk imagery. Lowering the gaze (24:30-31) makes the nudity gags a strong depiction concern.

frames.aligns: Karma-like chains of cause and effect, rebirth (Indra and Ashura), chakra as life energy, dharma as duty to community.
frames.concerns: Hindu names (Indra, asura, chakra) used loosely in a fighting story; some may see careless use of sacred terms.

frames.aligns: The "cycle of hatred" mirrors the teaching that hatred is not ended by hatred. Pain's six bodies are named for the six realms. Naruto's choice not to take revenge.
frames.concerns: Buddhist terms used as names of weapons and a villain's bodies; violence (first precept); intoxicants played for laughs (fifth precept).

frames.aligns: Kami names, harmony of the village and reverence for ancestors (the stone faces of past Hokage).
frames.concerns: Kami names (Amaterasu, Susanoo, Tsukuyomi, Izanagi) used as weapon names, which some may see as careless; death and blood without purification. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Overcoming ego (haumai) and anger; forgiveness over revenge; protecting the weak.
frames.concerns: Lust played as comedy (Jiraiya); drinking and gambling. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Unity of nations and the end of war; overcoming prejudice between clans; forgiveness.
frames.concerns: Degrading humor against a "chaste and holy life"; drinking and gambling (both forbidden); summoning. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Basically good beings capable of change; survival of the group; honoring teachers and parents.
frames.concerns: Orochimaru's human experiments shown as evil (fits); violence; drinking. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Nature energy (Sage Mode); bonds with animal spirits; harm ended through understanding.
frames.concerns: Constant fighting against "harm none"; Hidan's cult as the only explicit religion is a villain's. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: An outcast's dignity, empathy for enemies, criticism of war, secret police and clan discrimination.
frames.concerns: CSM flags sexism, fatphobia, disability clichés and the Killer Bee stereotype. Child soldiers as normal. Women end as wives and mothers (ch. 699-700). Harassment humor.

frames.aligns: Peace comes from people understanding each other, with no god intervening; reason and empathy defeat ideology (Pain, Madara).
frames.concerns: Destiny and bloodline (the reincarnation reveal) cut against self-made achievement.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, duty to community, respect for teachers and elders, courage, inherited "Will of Fire," marriage and children at the end.
frames.concerns: A "pervert" mentor shown as wise; drinking and gambling; a hero who defies superiors.

frames.aligns: An outcast who becomes his own master; secret authority (Danzo) exposed.
frames.concerns: The story's central rejection of revenge cuts against Church of Satan teaching on retaliation; The Satanic Temple's compassion tenets fit better. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of an outcast; justice and peace; understanding across difference.
frames.concerns: Stereotypes and gender roles CSM flags. (from general knowledge; to verify)

Dignity vs honor.evidence: The cycle of revenge is the central problem; Naruto refuses revenge on Pain (ch. 443-453) and refuses to kill Sasuke (ch. 694-699). Winning recognition through effort and keeping one's word are still honored.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Loyalty to the village, respect for teachers and sacrifice for the community are presented as right (Socio-cultural lens). Secret authoritarian rule is critiqued (Danzo, ch. 481; the Uchiha massacre order, ch. 224-225).

Civic vs kin.evidence: The village comes before the clan: the Uchiha coup is the tragedy Itachi stops (vol. 43). Bloodlines still carry inherited powers, and the ending settles the cast into families (ch. 700).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Becoming Hokage is the dream (ch. 700); teachers and the Hokage line are honored, and ninja ranks structure life. Hidden heritage and bloodline decide much of the outcome (Pragmatic lens).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Shinto deity names and Buddhist ideas (the Sage of Six Paths, ch. 671; reincarnated souls) shape the world, though no one prays. The ending shifts toward destiny and myth (Shifts).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: War and sacrifice for the village dominate Part II. Naruto's drive to be acknowledged, and the peace he wins, give some place to self-expression.

folkways.japan: Group loyalty, respect for teachers (sensei and senpai-kohai bonds), duty to the village and the conservative gender roles of the ending reflect postwar Japanese norms; Kishimoto's "war is never the right answer," credited to his grandfather, reflects Japan's postwar pacifism.

entry.dominant: Communitarianism (village and "Will of Fire"), Dharmic (Buddhist cycle of hatred), Classical virtue ethics, Confucian ethics. Lens labels are this entry's framing unless a source is named. Wikipedia's Naruto article notes Confucian values (respect for teachers, filial duty, group over self); the other labels are this entry's own.

entry.title: Hell’s Paradise: Jigokuraku
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.premise: In Edo-period Japan, the condemned ninja Gabimaru is offered a pardon if he retrieves the elixir of immortality from the island of Shinsenkyo. Dignity vs honor.evidence: Martial pride and the tournament code of honor run through the series; Vegeta's bloodline pride drives his arc. The story also honors mercy (sparing Frieza) and Vegeta's turn from pride to self-sacrifice (ch. 467).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Goku fights for the joy of it and does not seek command; each arc's hero is stronger but chooses not to rule (Philosophy essay). Gods are bureaucrats and mentors, not lawgivers, and Goku leaves home to train Uub (ch. 517-519).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Goku protects Earth because his friends live there. Former enemies join the circle (Piccolo, Vegeta, Buu). Family is present but often secondary to friends and training.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Tyrants who want to own others are destroyed (Frieza, Cell, Kid Buu). Rank exists among fighters and gods (Kais, Supreme Kai), but strength is earned by training, and rivals are welcomed as equals.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: A Buddhist, Taoist and folk cosmology (King Yama, Kami, halos) is setting, not worship; Toriyama said he did not think deeply about it. Capsule Corp technology and whatever works solve problems (Pragmatic lens).

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Joyful striving is the life message: train, enjoy the fight, food and friends. Death is often reversible through the Dragon Balls, so security fears weigh lightly.

folkways.japan: The Jump formula of friendship, effort and victory, the master-and-disciple training model (Roshi, Kami) and the folk cosmology borrowed from Chinese and Japanese Buddhism reflect Japanese boys' manga norms of the 1980s and 1990s rather than the story's own argument.
